title: More weekly sets for a low-volume muscle
statement: In healthy adults training for muscle size (mostly young men, untrained or trained), more weekly sets per muscle give more muscle growth on average, but each extra set adds less than the one before. That supports raising a muscle from low volume (single sets, or under about 10 weekly sets) to about 10 weekly sets. Expect only a modest extra gain in size, with no promised strength benefit. Whether going above about 20 weekly sets adds anything more is uncertain.
population: Healthy adults doing resistance training to build muscle size. Most of the evidence comes from young men, both untrained and resistance-trained. Direct evidence in women, older adults and clinical groups was not verified, so the claim should not be presented as tested in those groups.
what_the_app_does: When a muscle gets fewer than 10 hard sets a week and you ask for it to grow, we can suggest adding sets toward 10, never above 20, within your session time.
supporting_source_ids: src-krieger-2010; src-schoenfeld-2017; src-pelland-2026; src-bernardez-vazquez-2022; src-schoenfeld-2019; src-radaelli-2015
verdict: Active. Six counted sources all point the same way: more volume gives more growth, with diminishing returns. They are the meta-analyses by Krieger 2010, Schoenfeld 2017 and Pelland 2026, the Bernárdez-Vázquez 2022 umbrella review, and the trials by Schoenfeld 2019 and Radaelli 2015. At least three of them come from independent research groups: Schoenfeld/Krieger, Pelland/Zourdos and Radaelli. The exact 10-set target comes from the umbrella review's conclusion and from the continuous dose-response models, not from a head-to-head trial. In Schoenfeld 2017 the under-10 versus 10+ category contrast was only a trend (P = 0.074). The main contrary result is Heaselgrave 2019: in trained men, 9 weekly biceps sets matched 18 or 27. But that trial covered one muscle over 6 weeks, mixed up volume with training frequency, and does not outweigh the pooled evidence. It, Baz-Valle 2022 and Schoenfeld 2019 (which favoured about 30+ sets) together leave the benefit above 20 sets uncertain.
evidence_gaps: 1. There is no head-to-head trial of about 5 to 9 versus 10 to 12 weekly sets per muscle, so the exact 10-set target rests on pooled trends and the umbrella review's conclusion. 2. Direct evidence in women, older adults and clinical groups was not verified. 3. These leads have not been checked yet: the ACSM 2026 position stand, Currier 2023 (the Br J Sports Med Bayesian network meta-analysis), Brigatto 2022 (PMID 31868813), Aubé 2022 (PMID 32058362) and Enes 2024 (PMID 37796222). If any of them showed no benefit from moving low volume up to about 10 sets, the status should be reconsidered. 4. No dedicated retraction check (for example Retraction Watch) was run on the eight sources, and the reportedly retracted Barbalho trials must not be used. 5. The effect above 20 weekly sets needs longer trials in trained people that do not mix up volume and frequency. Today those trials conflict: Schoenfeld 2019 against Heaselgrave 2019 and Baz-Valle 2022. 6. Several identifiers are still missing, such as the PMID for Bernárdez-Vázquez 2022. Most quotes were not seen word for word. 7. The strength outcome is mixed: Pelland 2026 found a positive slope with sharper diminishing returns, while Schoenfeld 2019 found no difference. The app should not claim any strength benefit from this claim.

title: Heavier loads for maximal strength
statement: In healthy adults, training with heavier loads (about 80% of 1RM or more, roughly 8 or fewer reps per set) gives larger gains in 1RM strength on the trained lifts than training with light loads (about 60% of 1RM or less, roughly 15 or more reps per set). An advantage over moderate loads (about 9-15 reps) is not established. When sets are taken to muscular failure, muscle growth is similar with light, moderate and heavy loads.
population: Healthy adults aged 18 and over. Most were young, untrained or recreationally trained, and more were men than women. The 1RM advantage of heavier loads was smaller in older adults (Refalo 2021: effect size 0.20 vs 0.34 in younger adults). Very few highly trained or elite athletes were studied, and the results in trained men are mixed: one RCT found load mostly did not change strength gains (Morton 2016), and a small RCT found larger squat gains with heavier loads (Schoenfeld 2015).
what_the_app_does: When you ask to get stronger, we can suggest heavier loads (about 8 reps or fewer) for main lifts you train with light loads (15 reps or more). We don't push lifts that are already moderate or heavy, because the evidence doesn't show that helps more.
supporting_source_ids: src-lopez-2021; src-currier-2023; src-refalo-2021; src-schoenfeld-2017-b; src-mcleod-2024; src-currier-2026; src-schoenfeld-2015
verdict: The narrowed claim is active. Seven counted sources support it, and five syntheses from at least four separate author groups agree that heavier loads give larger 1RM gains than light loads. These are Lopez 2021 and Currier 2023 (network meta-analyses), Refalo 2021 and Schoenfeld 2017 (pairwise meta-analyses) and Mcleod 2024 (umbrella review). The 2026 ACSM position stand and a small RCT (Schoenfeld 2015) back them up. The same syntheses find similar muscle growth across loads when sets go to failure. Morton 2016 runs against the strength half in trained men, and Hammert 2026 found the heavy-load edge on untested (isometric or isokinetic) strength inconclusive. Neither outweighs the pooled evidence, but they limit the claim to 1RM on the trained lifts. Lopez 2021 found moderate loads also beat light loads, so heavy over moderate, the specific 3-6 rep range, reps in reserve and rest lengths are not supported. The pairwise and network meta-analyses share many primary trials, and Currier 2023, Mcleod 2024 and ACSM 2026 come from overlapping McMaster authors, so the sources are less independent than their count suggests.
evidence_gaps: More evidence is needed in five areas. (1) Direct, volume-equated RCTs of heavy loads (about 3-6 reps) against moderate loads (about 8-12 reps), such as Mangine 2015 and Schoenfeld 2014 (not searched). These would be needed before the app could favour 3-6 reps over moderate loading. (2) Trials testing 2-3 reps in reserve and longer rests for strength. No verified source covers either, and the umbrella review found insufficient evidence on set end point and rest. (3) Evidence that similar growth across loads holds when sets stop short of failure. (4) More trials in trained and elite lifters, where results are mixed (Morton 2016 vs Schoenfeld 2015) and such lifters are about 2.3% of the evidence base. Also more trials in women and older adults, where the 1RM advantage looked smaller. (5) Better evidence on whether heavy-load gains carry over to strength tests that were not trained (Hammert 2026 was inconclusive). Several sources still need checking: Lopez 2021's effect sizes (high vs low SMD 0.60; high vs moderate non-significant) against its abstract or tables; ACSM 2026's PMID, abstract and hypertrophy recommendations; and the Currier 2023 and Mcleod 2024 identifiers on their own PubMed records. These leads were not verified or examined and were not used: Csapo & Alegre on older adults (PMID 26302881); the APNM volume-matched loads meta-analysis (doi 10.1139/apnm-2021-0515); the ACSM 2009 stand; the Schoenfeld 2016 Eur J Sport Sci meta-analysis (PMID 25530577); the 2026 paper on regional muscle and tendon growth (PMID 42319300), which may challenge similar growth in particular muscle regions; and a bioRxiv preprint. No dedicated retraction search was run for each paper.

title: Light or heavy loads grow muscle similarly
statement: In healthy young adults, training with loads from about 30% to about 85% of 1RM appears to give similar gains in whole-muscle size when sets are taken to momentary failure, while heavier loads still give larger gains in maximal (1RM) strength. This is not established for loads below about 30% of 1RM, or for light-load sets stopped well short of failure.
population: Healthy adults, untrained or resistance-trained. Most data come from young men aged about 18-35 in 6-12 week programmes. The claim is not established for women, older adults or highly trained athletes.
what_the_app_does: Would let us say that a change of load shouldn't cost you muscle. Until then, we don't say it.
context_source_ids: src-schoenfeld-2017-b; src-lopez-2021; src-refalo-2021; src-carvalho-2022; src-mcleod-2024; src-morton-2016; src-lees-2026; src-mitchell-2012; src-grgic-2020; src-lasevicius-2018
verdict: No source counts toward this claim. Verification of all 15 sources stopped when the shared web-search budget ran out, so no abstract or finding was checked against the claim, and every design, direction and finding check is unknown. The candidate evidence looks consistent: meta-analyses from four groups (Schoenfeld 2017, Lopez 2021, Refalo 2021, Carvalho 2022) and trials such as Mitchell 2012, Morton 2016 and Lees all report similar growth across loads. But the app's 3-source rule cannot be met until at least three of them pass verification. Even then the claim has limits: 20% 1RM gave about half the growth of 80% (Lasevicius 2018); light-load sets stopped short of failure appear to give less growth (Lasevicius 2022, identity not yet confirmed); fibre-level data lean non-significantly towards heavy loads (Grgic 2020); and heavier loads consistently give larger strength gains.
evidence_gaps: The decisive gap is verification, not evidence. Re-run verification in a turn with search budget available. At least three of Schoenfeld 2017, Lopez 2021, Refalo 2021, Carvalho 2022, Morton 2016, Lees and Mitchell 2012 must pass every check (identifier, metadata on a second independent page, peer review, retraction status, strong design, and a finding that supports the claim) before the status can be active. Because the meta-analyses share most of their primary trials, and Mitchell, Morton and Lees come from one laboratory, the counted set should include reviews from different groups, or at least one RCT from another laboratory (e.g. Schoenfeld 2015), so the agreement is not the same data counted twice. Lasevicius 2022 needs its identity confirmed to support the rule that light-load sets must end at or within about 1 rep of failure, and direct trials of light loads at 1-3 reps in reserve would be needed to extend the claim from 'to failure' to 'close to failure'. Lasevicius 2018 should be verified to fix the lower bound at about 30% 1RM. The upper bound above about 85-90% 1RM rests only on a small 2025 trial (Cumming et al.) with an unconfirmed PMID. Applying the claim beyond young men would need trials in women, older adults and highly trained athletes. The type II fibre question (Grgic 2020) remains open.

title: Spreading the same sets over more days
statement: In healthy adults, when weekly sets per muscle are kept the same, training a muscle once a week or spreading those sets over two or three sessions a week appears to give similar muscle growth. This has not yet been confirmed by verified sources, and no claim is made about strength.
population: Healthy adults, mostly young (pooled mean age about 25) and mostly male (about 79%), untrained or resistance-trained, doing supervised programmes of about 6 to 12 weeks (some up to about 30) at 1 to 3 sessions per muscle per week. The evidence does not reliably cover women, adults over 60, clinical groups, more than 3 sessions per muscle per week, or programmes much longer than 12 weeks.
what_the_app_does: Would let us move sets between days to fit your session time. Until then, we only move them when you edit your plan.
verdict: None of the nine candidate sources counts: the shared search budget ran out before any checks ran, so for every source the identity, peer-review status, retraction status, design and reported finding are all unknown. The submitted evidence looks consistent for hypertrophy (Schoenfeld 2019, Pelland 2026, Tao 2026, Ramos-Campo 2024 and Pedersen 2024 all report no meaningful difference at equal volume), but none of it is verified, so the claim must stay a draft. Two sources point the other way: Schoenfeld 2016 found twice a week beat once a week, and the small Zaroni 2019 trial found more growth with 5 sessions a week. Both favour more frequent training, so they do not suggest splitting sets would cause harm. The strength part, including the 'mainly through extra volume' clause, is contested: Grgic 2018 and Cuthbert 2021 found no volume-equated effect, while Tao 2026, Pelland 2026 and Pedersen 2024 report a small independent benefit. So it is left out of the statement.
evidence_gaps: 1) Verification has to be re-run, ideally in a turn with search budget left. At least 3 of Schoenfeld 2019, Pelland 2026, Tao 2026, Ramos-Campo 2024 and Pedersen 2024 must pass every check (identifier, metadata, peer review, no retraction, strong design) with a confirmed volume-equated hypertrophy finding. Specific items to resolve: the Grgic 2018 PMID conflict (29470825 vs 28444646), the journal and peer-review status of Tao 2026, the full citation for Pelland 2026, and whether every trial in Ramos-Campo 2024 equated volume. 2) The volume-equated RCTs the researcher cited (Hamarsland 2022, Gomes 2019, Saric 2019, Gentil 2018, Brigatto 2019) were never put forward for verification. Verifying them would add primary evidence that does not rely on overlapping meta-analyses. 3) Even once verified, the meta-analyses draw on the same pool of small trials and often share authors. At least one source from an independent group, or independent primary trials, would strengthen any activation. 4) Supporting 4 or more sessions per muscle per week would need more volume-equated trials at those frequencies. 5) Trials in women, adults over 60, clinical groups, and programmes longer than 12 weeks are needed before the claim can be extended to them. 6) A strength statement would need agreement between Grgic 2018 and Cuthbert 2021 on one side and Tao 2026, Pelland 2026 and Pedersen 2024 on the other. The question is whether frequency helps strength independently of volume or through extra practice of the tested lift. 7) No source gives a maximum number of sets per session, so the app has no basis for a per-session cap.

title: Stopping sets short of failure
statement: In healthy, mostly young adults, training to failure is not needed: stopping sets short of failure gives similar, and sometimes slightly greater, strength gains, and similar or only slightly smaller muscle growth. For muscle growth, ending sets closer to failure tends to give a little more growth; for strength, how close to failure sets end matters little.
population: Healthy adults, mostly young (about 18 to 35), both untrained and resistance-trained, in supervised programmes lasting roughly 6 to 14 weeks. Evidence in older adults and in highly trained or elite lifters is limited.
what_the_app_does: Explains why our plans never ask you to train to failure: stopping a little short works about as well.
verdict: Four counted sources support the narrowed claim. For strength, Grgic 2022, Davies 2016 and Robinson 2024 agree that stopping short of failure gives similar or slightly better gains. For muscle growth, Grgic 2022, Refalo 2023 and Robinson 2024 agree that failure gives at most a small advantage, and Robinson finds growth rises as sets end closer to failure. The main contrary evidence is Vieira 2021, which found a moderate growth advantage for failure (SMD 0.75); that advantage disappears when training volumes are matched, and it does not outweigh the larger, later analyses. The draft's '1 to 3 reps in reserve' range and the researcher's '0 to 2 RIR, 3 at most' limits are not set by any counted source, so those numbers are dropped. The reviews also share many of the same small, short trials, so they are less independent than four sources suggests.
evidence_gaps: 1. Specific reps-in-reserve targets need at least three counted sources that test or estimate outcomes at defined RIR values. Examples are head-to-head trials of about 1 to 3 RIR against failure for growth, or verified per-RIR predictions from the Robinson 2024 full text. No trial yet compares 3 RIR directly with 0 RIR for growth. 2. Verifying the Wu 2026 metadata (authors, volume, PMID) would add a fourth independent-analysis source for strength and growth. 3. Checking that limbs were randomly allocated in Refalo 2024 would let that trial count for the 1 to 2 RIR finding. 4. The content of the Davies 2016 erratum and of the comment on Refalo 2023 is unknown. 5. The reviews share many of the same primary trials, and Robinson 2024 shares authors and data with Refalo 2023. Independent, larger and longer trials (over 12 weeks) with measured rather than estimated RIR would strengthen the evidence. 6. Evidence is sparse for older adults and for highly trained or elite lifters, so the statement should not be extended to them without dedicated studies. 7. No dedicated retraction-database search was run.

title: Longer rests between sets
statement: When the number of sets stays the same, resting more than about 60 seconds between sets may give slightly more muscle growth than resting 60 seconds or less. There seems to be no clear extra benefit beyond about 90 seconds, and the difference is small and uncertain. For strength, resistance-trained lifters gain more with rests longer than about 2 minutes, while untrained people do about as well with 60-120 seconds.
population: Healthy adults doing resistance training, mostly young men. The finding that rests over 2 minutes help strength applies only to resistance-trained lifters. For untrained people, 60-120 seconds appears to be enough for strength. The evidence covers exercises in general and has nothing specific to multi-joint lifts. Women, older adults and programmes longer than about 10-12 weeks are barely represented.
what_the_app_does: Would let us suggest rest times between sets. Until then, your rests are whatever your plan says, and we use them only to estimate session length.
verdict: Draft. Only three sources pass every check (Singer 2024, Grgic 2018 and Schoenfeld 2016), and each backs a different part of the claim. Muscle growth is supported only by Singer 2024 (small effect, credible intervals crossing zero) and Schoenfeld 2016. Strength in trained lifters is supported only by Grgic 2018 and Schoenfeld 2016. So no single statement has three counted sources, and the Schoenfeld trial probably also sits inside both reviews, which share an author. The original draft's claim that 2 minutes or more gives more growth is not supported beyond about 90 seconds, and nothing isolates multi-joint lifts. Volume-matched trials (Longo 2022, Attarieh 2026) suggest any advantage comes from the extra volume that longer rests allow. Fink 2018 found the opposite, but rest was confounded with load. The ACSM 2026 stand reportedly found no strength effect of rest, but that is unverified.
evidence_gaps: The status could change to active if each part of the statement had at least 3 counted, reasonably independent sources. For muscle growth, a further strong source is needed. The status could change if randomisation is confirmed in Buresh 2009, if the Grgic 2017 abstract wording on trained participants is checked, or if a new well-powered randomised trial or independent meta-analysis with sets held equal is found. For strength in trained lifters, the lead PMID 19811949 (1, 3 and 5-minute rests in trained men) should be verified, along with any other independent randomised trial. The study lists of Singer 2024 and Grgic 2017/2018 need to be compared to see how far they reuse the same trials, including Schoenfeld 2016. The primary text of the ACSM 2026 stand must be checked: if it reports no effect of rest on strength, that would weigh against the claim. The following checks are still to do: the Attarieh 2026 correction, randomisation in Longo 2022, and dedicated retraction searches. No study compares multi-joint with single-joint exercises, so the draft's multi-joint wording cannot be tested. Data on women, older adults and training longer than about 12 weeks are needed before the claim is applied to those users.

title: Strength training on 2 or more days a week
statement: Not yet verified: WHO (2020) and US (2018) guidelines are reported to recommend that adults do muscle-strengthening activity on 2 or more days a week, alongside aerobic activity, and observational studies are reported to link any such activity with lower all-cause mortality. None of the sources has been verified, so this stays a draft and the app changes nothing.
population: Adults aged 18 and over in the general, non-clinical population. This is the proposed scope and has not been verified. The guideline part would cover adults aged 18 to 64 and those aged 65 and over. The mortality evidence would come mostly from middle-aged and older adults in prospective cohorts.
what_the_app_does: Would let us suggest a second strength day for the general health goal.
verdict: No source counts towards this claim. The shared web-search budget ran out before any check could run, so all 9 sources, including the two guidelines (Bull 2020, Piercy 2018) and the main meta-analyses (Momma 2022, Shailendra 2022, Saeidifard 2019), have every check marked unknown. With zero of the 3 required sources verified, the claim stays a draft, however plausible it is. Even the researcher's own description of the evidence would narrow the claim. It shows null or borderline results for cancer and cardiovascular mortality (Saeidifard 2019; Nascimento 2021 high vs low HR 0.87, 0.73-1.02), J- or U-shaped dose curves, no hard-outcome trials and heavy overlap between the meta-analyses.
evidence_gaps: 1) Verification has to run before anything else. At least 3 sources must pass every check (identifier, metadata, peer review, not retracted, strong design, finding supported) with the direction 'supports'. Re-check the most likely ones first: Bull 2020 (WHO) and Piercy 2018 (US PAG) for the 2-days-a-week recommendation, then Momma 2022, Shailendra 2022 and Saeidifard 2019 for the mortality link. Confirm the Shailendra PMID (35599175 vs 36528354) and look for retraction or correction notices on all of them. 2) Even if these pass, the statement probably needs narrowing. On the reported findings, the evidence is strongest for the guideline recommendation and for lower all-cause mortality. It is weak or null for total cancer mortality (Nascimento high vs low; Saeidifard) and borderline for cardiovascular mortality, so 'chronic disease' should not be stated without qualification. 3) The meta-analyses probably pool many of the same cohorts, and the guidelines draw on the same evidence base. A check of study-by-study overlap is needed before treating them as independent. 4) The pooled dose-response data is in minutes per week, not days per week. Direct evidence that 2 or more days beats 1 day exists only for total cancer mortality (Nascimento, HR 0.81), so the 2-day threshold rests on guideline consensus. 5) All hard-outcome evidence is observational and self-reported. Randomised trials, or well-controlled cohorts with device-measured activity, would be needed to support any causal framing. 6) The dose ceiling is uncertain: the reported peak is 30-60 min/week in Momma and about 60 min/week in Shailendra, against a plateau above 120 min/week in Zhang 2026. This needs resolving before the app sets any volume figure.

title: Planned lighter weeks
statement: Not established: there is no verified evidence that planned deload weeks improve strength or muscle gains compared with continuous resistance training.
population: Healthy adults doing resistance training. The trials, none of them verified yet, mostly studied untrained or detrained young adults. Only one studied resistance-trained adults (39 people). There are no data for older adults or competitive athletes, and none beyond 6 months.
what_the_app_does: Would let us suggest planned lighter (deload) weeks. Until then, we never add them.
context_source_ids: src-coleman-2024; src-pancar-2026; src-halonen-2024; src-ogasawara-2013; src-ogasawara-2011; src-gentil-2015; src-bosquet-2013; src-bell-2023; src-rogerson-2024
verdict: Draft: no source passed verification. The web search budget ran out before any identifier, metadata, retraction or design check could run, so 0 sources count against the 3 required. Even taken at face value, none of the reported trials shows a benefit, so the draft claim that deloads "improve" gains would fail anyway. The direct trials are Coleman 2024 and Pancar 2026. The break-versus-continuous trials are Ogasawara 2011 and 2013, Gentil 2015 and Halonen 2024. All report similar overall gains, and Coleman 2024 reports somewhat smaller lower-body strength gains after a full week off. The researcher's narrower "little or no cost, no benefit" statement cannot be activated until at least three of these trials pass verification. Coleman 2024's direction label is also inconsistent: it is labelled as contradicting, but its finding supports the narrower statement, so it needs rechecking.
evidence_gaps: Before any deload statement can become active, at least three trials must pass every check: PMID or DOI, metadata, peer review, retraction status, randomised design, and that the reported findings match the paper. The best candidates are Coleman 2024 (PMID 38274324 / PMC10809978), Pancar 2026 (a published record must first be found), Halonen 2024, Ogasawara 2013 and Gentil 2015. Ogasawara 2011 also needs its randomisation confirmed. Supporting the original claim that deloads improve gains would take something much stronger: randomised trials in resistance-trained lifters showing that roughly one-week reduced-volume deloads produce larger strength or muscle gains than continuous training, ideally pooled in a systematic review. Those trials would also need follow-up beyond 6 months and outcomes such as injury, overreaching and adherence. Registered trials NCT06825052 and NCT06573086 (TraDeRe2024) may help fill this gap.

verdict: We have not finished checking the evidence for this claim, so the app treats it as unsupported and changes nothing.
